newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Yen risk reversals relent, mark resilient.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Yen risk reversals relent, mark resilient.

text.p: A stubborn, sharp skew for yen calls in dollar/yen option risk reversals, the put/call pricing differential, appeared to be relenting at last as the dollar continued circling the 113-yen level, traders said.
Dollar/yen implied volatilities, which had been pumped up especially in shorter maturities, also softened as time-decay began to outweigh fears of another abrupt dollar slide, they added.
"There's finally a little bit of disappointment in dollar/yen," said Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A.

One-month 25-delta risk reversal, the cost of swapping equally out-of-the-money puts and calls, narrowed to about 2.0/2.4 percentage points after staying near 3.0 for about a week and actually trading at 3.0 on Monday.
One-month implied volatility eased to 10.5/10.7 percent by late morning U.S. from about 11.4/11.7 at Wednesday's close.
A U.S. bank trader in New York said yen calls that end-users had bought in the past few months were gradually maturing, relieving dealers' downside negative gamma risks.
"Market-makers' portfolios are not quite as exposed as they were," he said.
Still, Revercomb said it was still too early to call it "game over" because the yen tended to move discontinuously.

"It's important to keep perspective," he said, adding that risk reversals above two points would have seemed "astronomical" until a few months ago. He said dealers were reporting a fresh build-up in range binaries and short strangles, which were depressing volatilities now but could eventually catch fire should spot resume its downmove.
Dollar/mark volatilities were resilient, despite a pullback to the 1.75-mark area from a fresh 41-month high of 1.7665 marks touched overnight.
With volatilities still generally low from a historical perspective, traders were reluctant to go short.
"It (spot) is still moving around in a 150-point (1.50 pfennig) range," the bank trader said.
Most traders expected the dollar to continue grinding higher, keeping a mild upward pressure on volatilities.

"There's not a lot of risk holding 8.2-8.4 percent vols in dollar/mark (for delta-hedgers)," Revercomb said. "But you can't expect to generate a lot of vega gains (premium gains resulting from higher volatilities) because vols aren't going to get bid up until we reach some uncomfortable levels."

"Making new four-year highs on a daily basis by 20 ticks (0.2 pfennig) just won't do it," he added. "If you get toward 1.80 marks, you'll probably get a little bit of a pop out of that, but we're not going to see vols run away."
On the other hand, he noted, a downturn in the dollar, particularly if accompanied by a renewed selloff in dollar/yen, could spark bigger interest in volatilities.
One-month dollar/mark was steady at 8.3/8.5 percent.
Sterling volatilities edged down as spot cable and sterling/mark pulled back after a widely expected 25 basis point rate hike by the Bank of England earlier today.
-- Shin Kishima/Chicago Derivatives Desk ((312-408-8750))
E-mail: derivatives@reuters.com
